Algebra.title: Introduction to Algebra
Algebra.introduction: Algebra is a branch of mathematics that uses letters and symbols to represent numbers and unknown quantities. It helps us describe relationships and solve problems.
keyConcepts: A variable is a letter or symbol that represents an unknown or changing value, such as x.
A constant is a fixed number, such as 5 or 12.
A coefficient is the number multiplying a variable. In 4x, the coefficient is 4.
An algebraic expression contains numbers, variables and operations, but has no equality sign.
An equation states that two expressions are equal.
Like terms have the same variable raised to the same power and can be combined.

example.question: Solve the equation: 3x + 5 = 20.
example.solution: Subtract 5 from both sides: 3x = 15. Divide both sides by 3 to isolate x.

Algebra.summary: Algebra uses symbols to represent quantities. To solve a simple equation, use inverse operations on both sides to isolate the variable while keeping the equality balanced.

Trigonometry.title: Introduction to Trigonometry
Trigonometry.introduction: Trigonometry studies relationships between the angles and sides of triangles. In right-angled triangles, the sine, cosine and tangent ratios connect an angle to the lengths of its sides.
keyConcepts: A right-angled triangle contains one angle of 90 degrees.
The hypotenuse is the side opposite the right angle and is the longest side.
Relative to a chosen acute angle, the opposite side is across from the angle and the adjacent side is next to it.
Sine: sin(theta) = opposite / hypotenuse.
Cosine: cos(theta) = adjacent / hypotenuse.
Tangent: tan(theta) = opposite / adjacent.
The mnemonic SOH-CAH-TOA helps recall the three ratios.

example.question: A right-angled triangle has an angle of 30 degrees and a hypotenuse of 10 cm. Find the length of the side opposite the angle.
example.solution: Use sine: sin(30 degrees) = opposite / 10. Since sin(30 degrees) = 0.5, the opposite side = 10 x 0.5.
example.answer: The opposite side is 5 cm.

Trigonometry.summary: Trigonometric ratios are used to find unknown sides or angles in right-angled triangles. Identify the sides relative to the given angle, then choose sine, cosine or tangent.

Geometry.title: Introduction to Geometry
Geometry.introduction: Geometry is the branch of mathematics concerned with shapes, sizes, positions and properties of space. It includes plane shapes such as triangles and circles, as well as solid objects.
keyConcepts: A point indicates an exact position and has no dimensions.
A line extends endlessly in both directions; a line segment has two endpoints.
An angle is formed when two rays meet at a common endpoint.
The angles in a triangle add up to 180 degrees.
The perimeter of a plane shape is the total distance around its boundary.
The area of a rectangle is length multiplied by width.
The area of a triangle is one-half multiplied by base and perpendicular height.

example.question: A rectangle is 8 cm long and 5 cm wide. Find its perimeter and area.
example.solution: Perimeter = 2 x (length + width) = 2 x (8 + 5). Area = length x width = 8 x 5.
example.answer: Perimeter = 26 cm; area = 40 cm squared.

Geometry.summary: Geometry helps us describe and measure shapes. Remember to use the correct formula and include the appropriate units, such as cm for length and cm squared for area.

Fractions, Decimals and Percentages.title: Introduction to Fractions, Decimals and Percentages
Fractions, Decimals and Percentages.introduction: Fractions, decimals and percentages are three ways of writing parts of a whole. They can be converted from one form to another and are used daily in money, measurement and data.
keyConcepts: A fraction has a numerator (top) and a denominator (bottom); the denominator shows how many equal parts make the whole.
To add or subtract fractions, first write them with a common denominator.
To convert a fraction to a decimal, divide the numerator by the denominator.
A percentage means 'out of 100'. To convert a decimal to a percentage, multiply by 100.
To find a percentage of an amount, multiply the amount by the percentage divided by 100.
Percentage increase or decrease = (change / original value) x 100.
Equivalent fractions have the same value, for example 1/2 = 2/4 = 50/100.

example.question: A shirt costing GH₵80 is sold with a 15% discount. Find the discount and the new price.
example.solution: Discount = 15/100 x 80 = 12. New price = 80 - 12.
example.answer: The discount is GH₵12 and the new price is GH₵68.

Fractions, Decimals and Percentages.summary: Fractions, decimals and percentages describe the same quantities in different forms. Learning to convert between them makes calculations with money, discounts and data much easier.

Statistics.title: Introduction to Statistics
Statistics.introduction: Statistics is the branch of mathematics that involves collecting, organising, presenting and interpreting data. Measures of average summarise a set of data using a single representative value.
keyConcepts: The mean is the sum of all values divided by the number of values.
The median is the middle value when the data are arranged in order.
The mode is the value that occurs most often.
The range is the highest value minus the lowest value.
A frequency table shows how many times each value or class occurs.
Data can be displayed using bar charts, pie charts, histograms and line graphs.
If there is an even number of values, the median is the mean of the two middle values.

example.question: Find the mean, median, mode and range of: 4, 7, 7, 9, 13.
example.solution: Mean = (4 + 7 + 7 + 9 + 13) / 5 = 40 / 5. The middle value is 7. The value 7 appears twice. Range = 13 - 4.
example.answer: Mean = 8; median = 7; mode = 7; range = 9.

Statistics.summary: Mean, median and mode describe the centre of a data set, while the range describes its spread. Choosing a suitable chart helps to present data clearly.

Indices and Logarithms.title: Introduction to Indices and Logarithms
Indices and Logarithms.introduction: An index (or power) shows how many times a number is multiplied by itself. Logarithms are the inverse of indices and help us solve equations where the unknown is a power.
keyConcepts: In a^n, a is the base and n is the index (power).
Multiplication law: a^m x a^n = a^(m+n).
Division law: a^m / a^n = a^(m-n).
Power law: (a^m)^n = a^(mn).
Any non-zero number raised to the power 0 equals 1.
A negative index means a reciprocal: a^(-n) = 1 / a^n.
If a^x = N, then log base a of N = x.

example.question: Simplify 2^3 x 2^4 and write the answer as a single number.
example.solution: Add the indices because the bases are the same: 2^(3+4) = 2^7 = 128.

Indices and Logarithms.summary: Laws of indices simplify expressions with powers. Logarithms reverse the process of exponentiation and are useful for solving equations where the unknown is an index.

Sets and Probability.title: Introduction to Sets and Probability
Sets and Probability.introduction: A set is a collection of well-defined objects. Probability measures how likely it is that an event will happen, using a number from 0 to 1.
keyConcepts: A set is written using curly brackets, for example {2, 4, 6}.
The union of two sets contains all elements that are in either set.
The intersection of two sets contains the elements found in both sets.
The universal set contains all the elements being considered.
Probability of an event = number of favourable outcomes / total number of possible outcomes.
A probability of 0 means impossible and a probability of 1 means certain.
The probabilities of all possible outcomes of an experiment add up to 1.

example.question: A bag has 3 red, 5 blue and 2 green balls. One ball is picked at random. Find the probability that it is blue.
example.solution: Total balls = 3 + 5 + 2 = 10. Favourable outcomes = 5. Probability = 5 / 10.
example.answer: The probability is 1/2 (or 0.5).

Sets and Probability.summary: Sets organise objects into groups, and Venn diagrams show how groups overlap. Probability compares favourable outcomes with all possible outcomes.

Motion.title: Introduction to Motion
Motion.introduction: Motion is the change in the position of an object with time, relative to a reference point. We describe motion using quantities such as distance, displacement, speed, velocity and acceleration.
keyConcepts: Distance is the total length of the path travelled. It is a scalar quantity and is measured in metres (m).
Displacement is the straight-line change in position in a specified direction. It is a vector quantity.
Average speed = total distance travelled / total time taken.
Average velocity = displacement / time taken.
Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity with time. Its SI unit is metres per second squared (m/s squared).
An object has uniform velocity when its speed and direction remain constant.
A reference point is a position used to decide whether an object has changed location.

example.question: A student walks 120 metres in 30 seconds at a steady pace. Calculate the student's average speed.
example.solution: Average speed = distance / time = 120 m / 30 s.
example.answer: Average speed = 4 m/s.

Motion.summary: Motion describes a change in position over time. Distance and speed are scalars, while displacement and velocity include direction. Acceleration describes how quickly velocity changes.

Forces.title: Introduction to Forces
Forces.introduction: A force is a push or pull that can change an object's motion, direction or shape. Forces are vector quantities, so they have both magnitude and direction.
keyConcepts: The SI unit of force is the newton (N).
A balanced set of forces has zero resultant force and does not cause a change in an object's velocity.
An unbalanced resultant force causes an object to accelerate.
Newton's First Law states that an object remains at rest or moves at constant velocity unless acted on by a resultant external force.
Newton's Second Law is expressed as resultant force = mass x acceleration (F = ma).
Newton's Third Law states that when one object exerts a force on another, the second exerts an equal-sized force in the opposite direction on the first.
Friction opposes relative motion between surfaces in contact.

example.question: A resultant force of 12 N acts on a 3 kg object. Calculate its acceleration.
example.solution: Using F = ma, rearrange to a = F / m. Therefore a = 12 N / 3 kg.
example.answer: Acceleration = 4 m/s squared.

Forces.summary: Forces can change motion or shape. The effect of a resultant force depends on its size, direction and the mass of the object. Newton's laws describe important relationships between forces and motion.

Energy.title: Introduction to Energy
Energy.introduction: Energy is the capacity to do work or cause change. It exists in different forms and can be transferred from one object or system to another.
keyConcepts: The SI unit of energy is the joule (J).
Kinetic energy is the energy an object has because it is moving.
Gravitational potential energy is energy stored because of an object's position in a gravitational field.
Thermal energy is associated with the random motion and interactions of particles.
Chemical energy is stored in substances such as food, fuels and batteries.
The principle of conservation of energy states that energy cannot be created or destroyed; it is transferred or transformed.
Power is the rate at which energy is transferred or work is done. Its SI unit is the watt (W).

example.question: A machine transfers 600 joules of energy in 20 seconds. Calculate its average power.
example.solution: Power = energy transferred / time taken = 600 J / 20 s.
example.answer: Average power = 30 W.

Energy.summary: Energy occurs in many forms and is transferred during changes. Total energy is conserved, although some energy may become less useful, for example when dissipated to the surroundings as thermal energy.

Electricity.title: Introduction to Electricity
Electricity.introduction: Electricity involves the flow of electric charge, usually electrons, around a complete circuit. Current, potential difference and resistance are linked by Ohm's law.
keyConcepts: Electric current is the rate of flow of charge. Its SI unit is the ampere (A).
Potential difference (voltage) is the energy transferred per unit charge. Its SI unit is the volt (V).
Resistance opposes the flow of current. Its SI unit is the ohm.
Ohm's law: V = I x R, for a conductor at constant temperature.
In a series circuit, the same current flows through every component and the voltages add up.
In a parallel circuit, the voltage across each branch is the same and the branch currents add up.
Electrical power: P = I x V.

example.question: A 12 V battery is connected to a resistor of 4 ohms. Calculate the current.
example.solution: Using V = IR, I = V / R = 12 / 4.
example.answer: The current is 3 A.

Electricity.summary: Current flows in a complete circuit when there is a potential difference. Ohm's law links voltage, current and resistance, and circuits can be arranged in series or in parallel.

Waves and Sound.title: Introduction to Waves and Sound
Waves and Sound.introduction: A wave transfers energy from one place to another without transferring matter. Sound is a longitudinal wave that needs a medium to travel through.
keyConcepts: Amplitude is the maximum displacement of a wave from its rest position.
Wavelength is the distance between two consecutive identical points on a wave.
Frequency is the number of waves passing a point each second. Its unit is the hertz (Hz).
Wave speed: v = f x wavelength.
In transverse waves, particles vibrate at right angles to the direction of travel; in longitudinal waves they vibrate parallel to it.
Sound cannot travel through a vacuum.
Pitch depends on frequency and loudness depends on amplitude.

example.question: A wave has a frequency of 50 Hz and a wavelength of 6 m. Calculate its speed.
example.solution: v = f x wavelength = 50 x 6.
example.answer: The wave speed is 300 m/s.

Waves and Sound.summary: Waves carry energy and are described by amplitude, wavelength, frequency and speed. Sound is a longitudinal wave whose pitch and loudness depend on frequency and amplitude.

Light.title: Introduction to Light
Light.introduction: Light is a form of energy that travels as a transverse wave and allows us to see. It travels in straight lines and can be reflected and refracted.
keyConcepts: Light travels at about 300,000,000 m/s in a vacuum.
Law of reflection: the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection.
Refraction is the change in direction of light when it passes from one medium to another.
A plane mirror forms an image that is virtual, upright and the same size as the object.
A convex (converging) lens brings parallel rays together at the focal point.
White light can be split into a spectrum of colours by a prism, a process called dispersion.
Opaque materials block light, transparent materials allow light through, and translucent materials let some light pass.

example.question: A ray of light strikes a plane mirror at an angle of incidence of 35 degrees. What is the angle of reflection?
example.solution: By the law of reflection, the angle of reflection equals the angle of incidence.
example.answer: The angle of reflection is 35 degrees.

Light.summary: Light travels in straight lines and can be reflected and refracted. Mirrors and lenses use these properties to form images, and prisms show that white light is made of many colours.

Heat and Temperature.title: Introduction to Heat and Temperature
Heat and Temperature.introduction: Heat is energy transferred because of a temperature difference, while temperature measures how hot or cold something is. Heat flows from hotter regions to colder regions.
keyConcepts: Temperature is measured in degrees Celsius (C) or kelvin (K).
To convert Celsius to kelvin, add 273.
Conduction is heat transfer through a solid by particle vibrations; metals are good conductors.
Convection is heat transfer in liquids and gases by the movement of fluid.
Radiation is heat transfer by infrared waves and needs no medium.
Specific heat capacity is the energy needed to raise 1 kg of a substance by 1 degree Celsius.
Energy change: Q = m x c x (change in temperature).

example.question: How much energy is needed to raise the temperature of 2 kg of water by 10 degrees C? (Specific heat capacity of water = 4200 J/kg per degree C.)
example.solution: Q = m x c x change in temperature = 2 x 4200 x 10.

Heat and Temperature.summary: Heat moves by conduction, convection and radiation. The energy needed to change the temperature of a substance depends on its mass, its specific heat capacity and the temperature change.

Atomic Structure.title: Introduction to Atomic Structure
Atomic Structure.introduction: All ordinary matter is made from atoms. An atom has a small, dense nucleus containing protons and neutrons, with electrons occupying regions around the nucleus.
keyConcepts: A proton has a positive charge and is found in the nucleus.
A neutron has no electric charge and is found in the nucleus.
An electron has a negative charge and occupies the space around the nucleus.
The atomic number is the number of protons in an atom. It identifies the element.
The mass number is the total number of protons and neutrons in the nucleus.
In a neutral atom, the number of electrons equals the number of protons.
Isotopes are atoms of the same element with the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons.

example.question: A neutral atom has atomic number 11 and mass number 23. How many protons, electrons and neutrons does it have?
example.solution: Protons = atomic number = 11. A neutral atom has the same number of electrons as protons, so electrons = 11. Neutrons = mass number - atomic number = 23 - 11.
example.answer: 11 protons, 11 electrons and 12 neutrons.

Atomic Structure.summary: Atoms contain protons, neutrons and electrons. The number of protons determines the element, while the mass number counts protons and neutrons together.

Bonding.title: Introduction to Chemical Bonding
Bonding.introduction: Chemical bonding explains how atoms join together to form molecules and compounds. Atoms bond through interactions involving their outer-shell electrons, producing more stable arrangements.
keyConcepts: Ionic bonding involves the transfer of electrons, usually from a metal atom to a non-metal atom, forming oppositely charged ions that attract.
Covalent bonding involves atoms sharing pairs of electrons, commonly between non-metals.
A metallic bond is the attraction between positive metal ions and delocalised electrons.
An ion is an atom or group of atoms with an overall electric charge.
A cation is a positively charged ion; an anion is a negatively charged ion.
The properties of a substance, such as melting point and electrical conductivity, are influenced by its bonding and structure.

example.question: Explain how sodium and chlorine form sodium chloride (NaCl).
example.solution: A sodium atom transfers one outer electron to a chlorine atom. Sodium becomes a positively charged Na+ ion, while chlorine becomes a negatively charged Cl- ion. The oppositely charged ions attract each other.
example.answer: Sodium chloride forms through ionic bonding between Na+ and Cl- ions.

Bonding.summary: The main types of chemical bonding include ionic, covalent and metallic bonding. They differ in how electrons are transferred, shared or delocalised, and these differences help explain material properties.

Acids and Bases.title: Introduction to Acids and Bases
Acids and Bases.introduction: Acids and bases are important groups of substances with characteristic chemical properties. They can be identified using indicators and can react with each other in neutralisation reactions.
keyConcepts: In aqueous solution, an acid produces hydrogen ions (H+).
A base neutralises an acid; a soluble base is called an alkali.
Alkalis produce hydroxide ions (OH-) in aqueous solution.
The pH scale commonly runs from 0 to 14: values below 7 are acidic, 7 is neutral and values above 7 are alkaline at room temperature.
Litmus turns red in acidic solutions and blue in alkaline solutions.
Neutralisation is the reaction between an acid and a base to form a salt and water.
The general ionic equation for neutralisation is H+ + OH- -> H2O.

example.question: What products are formed when hydrochloric acid reacts completely with sodium hydroxide?
example.solution: This is a neutralisation reaction: hydrochloric acid + sodium hydroxide -> sodium chloride + water. The salt is formed from the metal ion and the acid's negative ion.
example.answer: Sodium chloride and water are formed.

Acids and Bases.summary: Acids and alkalis can be tested with indicators and described using the pH scale. When an acid reacts with a base, neutralisation produces a salt and water.

The Periodic Table.title: Introduction to the Periodic Table
The Periodic Table.introduction: The periodic table arranges elements in order of increasing atomic number. Elements with similar properties are placed in the same vertical column, called a group.
keyConcepts: Rows in the periodic table are called periods; columns are called groups.
Elements in the same group have the same number of outer-shell electrons and similar chemical properties.
Group 1 elements are the alkali metals; they are soft, reactive and become more reactive down the group.
Group 7 elements are the halogens; they become less reactive down the group.
Group 0 elements are the noble gases; they are unreactive because their outer shells are full.
Metals are found on the left and centre of the table; non-metals are on the right.
The period number equals the number of occupied electron shells.

example.question: Sodium has atomic number 11. In which group and period is it found?
example.solution: The electron arrangement is 2, 8, 1. There is 1 outer electron, so it is in Group 1. There are 3 occupied shells, so it is in Period 3.
example.answer: Sodium is in Group 1, Period 3.

The Periodic Table.summary: The position of an element in the periodic table is linked to its electron arrangement. Group number shows the outer electrons and period number shows the number of shells.

Rates of Reaction.title: Introduction to Rates of Reaction
Rates of Reaction.introduction: The rate of a reaction is how quickly reactants are used up or products are formed. Reactions happen when particles collide with enough energy.
keyConcepts: Rate = amount of reactant used or product formed / time taken.
Increasing temperature makes particles move faster, so collisions are more frequent and more energetic.
Increasing concentration means more particles in the same volume, giving more frequent collisions.
Increasing surface area (smaller pieces) exposes more particles to react.
A catalyst speeds up a reaction without being used up.
Increasing the pressure of gaseous reactants increases the rate of reaction.
Activation energy is the minimum energy colliding particles need to react.

example.question: Why does powdered calcium carbonate react faster with acid than the same mass of marble chips?
example.solution: Powder has a much larger surface area, so more particles are exposed to the acid and collisions happen more often.
example.answer: The powder has a larger surface area, giving more frequent collisions and a faster rate.

Rates of Reaction.summary: Reaction rate increases with higher temperature, concentration, pressure and surface area, or when a catalyst is used. All of these increase the frequency of successful collisions.

Introduction to Organic Chemistry.title: Introduction to Organic Chemistry
Introduction to Organic Chemistry.introduction: Organic chemistry is the study of compounds of carbon. Hydrocarbons are the simplest organic compounds and contain only carbon and hydrogen.
keyConcepts: Alkanes are saturated hydrocarbons with only single bonds; general formula CnH(2n+2).
Alkenes are unsaturated hydrocarbons containing a carbon-carbon double bond; general formula CnH2n.
The first four alkanes are methane, ethane, propane and butane.
Alkenes decolourise bromine water; alkanes do not.
Crude oil is separated into useful fractions by fractional distillation.
Complete combustion of a hydrocarbon produces carbon dioxide and water.
A homologous series is a family of compounds with the same general formula and similar chemical properties.

example.question: Write the molecular formula of an alkane with 5 carbon atoms.
example.solution: Use CnH(2n+2) with n = 5: H = 2(5) + 2 = 12.
example.answer: C5H12 (pentane).

Introduction to Organic Chemistry.summary: Alkanes and alkenes are hydrocarbons in different homologous series. Alkenes are more reactive because of their double bond, which can be shown by the bromine water test.

Cells.title: Introduction to Cells
Cells.introduction: The cell is the basic structural and functional unit of life. Living organisms may consist of one cell or many cells, and different cell structures carry out different functions.
keyConcepts: The cell membrane controls the movement of substances into and out of the cell.
The cytoplasm is where many chemical reactions take place.
The nucleus contains genetic material and helps control cell activities in many cells.
Mitochondria are the main site of aerobic respiration, which releases energy for cell activities.
Plant cells have a cellulose cell wall that supports and strengthens the cell.
Chloroplasts contain chlorophyll and are the site of photosynthesis in green plant cells.
A large permanent vacuole in many plant cells contains cell sap and helps maintain support.

example.question: A student observes a cell with a cell wall, chloroplasts and a large permanent vacuole. Is it most likely a plant or animal cell? Give a reason.
example.solution: These structures are characteristic features of many plant cells. Animal cells do not have a cellulose cell wall or chloroplasts.
example.answer: It is a plant cell because it has a cell wall, chloroplasts and a large permanent vacuole.

Cells.summary: Cells are the basic units of life. Their structures are adapted to their functions, and plant cells have additional structures such as a cell wall and chloroplasts.

Nutrition.title: Introduction to Nutrition
Nutrition.introduction: Nutrition is the process by which organisms obtain and use food or nutrients for energy, growth, repair and healthy functioning. Humans need a balanced diet containing different nutrients.
keyConcepts: Carbohydrates are an important source of energy.
Proteins are needed for growth and repair of body tissues.
Fats provide energy, help insulate the body and form part of cell membranes.
Vitamins and minerals are needed in small amounts for normal body processes.
Fibre supports healthy movement of food through the digestive system.
Water is needed for transport, chemical reactions and temperature regulation.
A balanced diet provides appropriate amounts of the nutrients and energy a person needs.

example.question: A meal contains rice, beans, vegetables and water. Identify two nutrients supplied by this meal and state one function of each.
example.solution: Rice supplies carbohydrates, which provide energy. Beans supply protein, which supports growth and tissue repair. Vegetables can supply vitamins, minerals and fibre.
example.answer: Carbohydrates provide energy; proteins support growth and repair. The vegetables also contribute vitamins, minerals and fibre.

Nutrition.summary: A balanced diet contains a variety of nutrients. Each nutrient has important functions, and eating a varied diet helps support growth, energy needs and general health.

Genetics.title: Introduction to Genetics
Genetics.introduction: Genetics is the study of heredity and variation. Heredity is the passing of characteristics from parents to offspring through genetic information.
keyConcepts: DNA is the molecule that carries hereditary information in most organisms.
A gene is a section of DNA that contributes to a particular characteristic or biological function.
Chromosomes are structures made of DNA and proteins that carry genes.
Alleles are different versions of the same gene.
An organism's genotype is its genetic make-up for a particular gene or set of genes.
A phenotype is an observable characteristic resulting from the interaction of genotype and environment.
In a simple dominant-recessive pattern, a dominant allele can determine the phenotype when one copy is present; a recessive phenotype usually requires two recessive alleles.

example.question: In a simple inheritance example, T represents a dominant allele for tall plants and t represents a recessive allele for short plants. What is the phenotype of a plant with genotype Tt?
example.solution: The plant has one dominant T allele and one recessive t allele. In this simple dominant-recessive example, the dominant allele determines the expressed characteristic.
example.answer: The plant is tall.

Genetics.summary: Genes and alleles carry inherited information. Genotype describes genetic make-up, while phenotype describes observable characteristics. Inheritance patterns explain some, but not all, variation among organisms.

Photosynthesis.title: Introduction to Photosynthesis
Photosynthesis.introduction: Photosynthesis is the process by which green plants use light energy to make glucose from carbon dioxide and water, releasing oxygen as a by-product.
keyConcepts: Word equation: carbon dioxide + water -> glucose + oxygen, in the presence of light and chlorophyll.
Chlorophyll absorbs light energy and is found in chloroplasts.
Carbon dioxide enters leaves through stomata.
Water is absorbed by roots and transported to the leaves through the xylem.
Glucose may be used for respiration, converted to starch for storage, or used to make cellulose, proteins and fats.
Limiting factors of photosynthesis include light intensity, carbon dioxide concentration and temperature.
A leaf tested with iodine solution turns blue-black if starch is present.

example.question: State two ways in which a leaf is adapted for photosynthesis.
example.solution: Leaves are thin and flat, giving a large surface area and a short diffusion distance. They also contain many chloroplasts and have stomata for gas exchange.
example.answer: A large surface area and many chloroplasts (or stomata for gas exchange).

Photosynthesis.summary: Photosynthesis converts light energy into chemical energy stored in glucose. It needs light, chlorophyll, carbon dioxide and water, and releases oxygen.

Respiration.title: Introduction to Respiration
Respiration.introduction: Respiration is the chemical process in living cells that releases energy from food molecules such as glucose. This energy is used for movement, growth, warmth and other life processes.
keyConcepts: Aerobic respiration uses oxygen: glucose + oxygen -> carbon dioxide + water + energy.
Anaerobic respiration releases energy without oxygen and releases less energy than aerobic respiration.
In muscles, anaerobic respiration produces lactic acid.
In yeast, anaerobic respiration (fermentation) produces ethanol and carbon dioxide.
Respiration is different from breathing: breathing is the movement of air in and out of the lungs.
Mitochondria are the site of most aerobic respiration in cells.
During vigorous exercise, an oxygen debt can build up and must be repaid afterwards.

example.question: Name the products of anaerobic respiration in human muscle cells.
example.solution: In muscle cells without enough oxygen, glucose is partly broken down into lactic acid, releasing a small amount of energy.
example.answer: Lactic acid (and a small amount of energy).

Respiration.summary: Respiration releases usable energy from food. Aerobic respiration releases much more energy than anaerobic respiration and produces carbon dioxide and water.

Ecology.title: Introduction to Ecology
Ecology.introduction: Ecology is the study of how living organisms interact with each other and with their physical environment. Energy and nutrients flow through ecosystems.
keyConcepts: An ecosystem is a community of living organisms interacting with their non-living environment.
A habitat is the place where an organism lives.
Producers (green plants) make their own food by photosynthesis.
Consumers obtain energy by eating other organisms: primary, secondary and tertiary consumers.
A food chain shows the transfer of energy; arrows point in the direction energy flows.
Only about 10 percent of energy is passed on at each trophic level.
Decomposers break down dead matter and return nutrients to the soil.

example.question: In the food chain grass -> grasshopper -> frog -> snake, identify the producer and the secondary consumer.
example.solution: Grass makes its own food, so it is the producer. The grasshopper is the primary consumer and the frog, which eats the grasshopper, is the secondary consumer.
example.answer: Producer: grass. Secondary consumer: frog.

Ecology.summary: Ecosystems depend on energy from the Sun captured by producers. Energy decreases along food chains, while decomposers recycle nutrients.

Grammar.title: Introduction to English Grammar
Grammar.introduction: Grammar is the system of rules that helps us arrange words into clear and meaningful sentences. It includes parts of speech, sentence structure, tense and punctuation.
keyConcepts: A noun names a person, place, thing or idea.
A pronoun takes the place of a noun, for example he, she, it or they.
A verb expresses an action or state of being.
An adjective describes a noun or pronoun.
An adverb modifies a verb, adjective or another adverb.
A preposition shows a relationship, often involving place, time or direction.
A conjunction connects words, phrases or clauses.
A complete sentence normally contains a subject and a verb and expresses a complete thought.

example.question: Identify the parts of speech of the words in this sentence: 'The diligent student answered quickly.'
example.solution: 'The' is a determiner, 'diligent' is an adjective, 'student' is a noun, 'answered' is a verb, and 'quickly' is an adverb.
example.answer: The sentence contains a determiner, adjective, noun, verb and adverb.

Grammar.summary: Grammar helps us communicate clearly. Understanding parts of speech and sentence structure makes speaking and writing more accurate and effective.

Comprehension.title: Reading Comprehension Skills
Comprehension.introduction: Reading comprehension is the ability to understand, interpret and respond to a written passage. It involves identifying information, recognising the writer's ideas and making reasonable inferences.
keyConcepts: Skimming means reading quickly to understand the general idea of a passage.
Scanning means searching for a specific detail, such as a name, date or figure.
The main idea is the central point the passage communicates.
Supporting details explain or provide evidence for the main idea.
An inference is a conclusion drawn from clues in the passage and what the reader already knows.
Context clues are nearby words or sentences that help explain an unfamiliar word.
Answers should be based on evidence from the passage and should follow the wording and instructions of the question.

example.question: Read this sentence: 'Although the sky was cloudy, Ama carried her umbrella because the weather report predicted rain.' Why did Ama carry an umbrella?
example.solution: Look for the stated reason in the sentence. It says the weather report predicted rain.
example.answer: Ama carried an umbrella because the weather report predicted rain.

Comprehension.summary: Good comprehension involves reading carefully, identifying main ideas, locating supporting details and making inferences from evidence. Always answer the question asked and support your response with the passage.

Summary Writing.title: Introduction to Summary Writing
Summary Writing.introduction: Summary writing is the skill of presenting the main ideas of a passage briefly and accurately in your own words. A good summary keeps essential information and leaves out unnecessary details.
keyConcepts: Read the passage carefully to understand its overall meaning.
Identify the main points that directly answer the task.
Leave out examples, repetition, illustrations and minor details unless they are essential.
Use your own words while preserving the original meaning.
Write clearly and logically, using suitable linking words where needed.
Avoid adding personal opinions or information that is not in the passage.
Follow the required word limit and check grammar, spelling and punctuation.

example.question: Original ideas: 'Regular exercise strengthens the heart. It can improve sleep. It also helps people manage stress.' Write a concise summary.
example.solution: Combine the three related benefits into one sentence without repeating the original wording.
example.answer: Regular physical activity benefits health by supporting heart function, sleep and stress management.

Summary Writing.summary: An effective summary is brief, accurate and written in your own words. It includes only the essential points, follows the task and avoids unnecessary details or personal opinions.

Essay Writing.title: Introduction to Essay Writing
Essay Writing.introduction: An essay is a structured piece of writing on a particular topic. A good essay has a clear introduction, well-developed body paragraphs and a conclusion.
keyConcepts: Plan before writing: choose the type of essay, list your main points and arrange them in order.
The introduction presents the topic and catches the reader's interest.
Each body paragraph develops one main idea, usually beginning with a topic sentence.
Support each point with explanations, examples or evidence.
The conclusion sums up the main points without introducing new ideas.
Common types include narrative, descriptive, argumentative, expository and discursive essays.
Use linking words such as however, therefore, in addition and finally to connect ideas.

example.question: Write a suitable topic sentence for a paragraph about the importance of reading.
example.solution: A topic sentence states the main idea of the paragraph so that the following sentences can explain or support it.
example.answer: Reading regularly improves a student's vocabulary, understanding and imagination.

Essay Writing.summary: Strong essays are planned, organised into paragraphs and written in clear, accurate language. Each paragraph should focus on one main idea and connect smoothly to the next.

Letter Writing.title: Introduction to Letter Writing
Letter Writing.introduction: Letters are written to communicate with individuals or organisations. Formal letters follow a fixed layout and polite, direct language, while informal letters are written to friends and family.
keyConcepts: A formal letter includes the sender's address, the date, the receiver's address, a salutation, a subject heading, the body and a closing.
Use 'Dear Sir/Madam' when the name is unknown and close with 'Yours faithfully'.
Use 'Dear Mr/Ms Surname' when the name is known and close with 'Yours sincerely'.
Formal letters use polite, standard English with no slang or contractions.
An informal letter uses a friendly tone and may include personal news.
The body of a formal letter should state the purpose in the first paragraph.
Proofread for spelling, grammar and punctuation before sending.

example.question: Which closing should be used for a formal letter beginning 'Dear Sir'?
example.solution: A letter beginning with 'Dear Sir' does not use a personal name, so the matching formal closing is 'Yours faithfully'.
example.answer: Yours faithfully.

Letter Writing.summary: Formal letters follow a set layout and polite tone, whereas informal letters are relaxed and personal. Match the salutation and closing to the type of letter.

Figures of Speech.title: Introduction to Figures of Speech
Figures of Speech.introduction: Figures of speech are expressions that use words in a non-literal way to create vivid images, emphasis or effect. They are common in poetry, prose and everyday speech.
keyConcepts: A simile compares two different things using 'like' or 'as', for example 'as brave as a lion'.
A metaphor states that one thing is another, for example 'Time is a thief'.
Personification gives human qualities to non-human things.
Hyperbole is deliberate exaggeration for effect.
Alliteration is the repetition of the same initial consonant sound in nearby words.
Onomatopoeia is a word that imitates a sound, such as 'buzz' or 'crash'.
An idiom is a fixed expression whose meaning is not obvious from the individual words.

example.question: Name the figure of speech in: 'The wind whispered through the trees.'
example.solution: The wind is given the human action of whispering, so human qualities are given to a non-human thing.
example.answer: Personification.

Figures of Speech.summary: Figures of speech make language more expressive. Learn to identify them and to explain the effect they create in a text.

Map Reading.title: Introduction to Map Reading
Map Reading.introduction: A map is a drawing of an area as seen from above, drawn to scale. Map-reading skills help us find places, measure distances and understand the landscape.
keyConcepts: A scale shows the relationship between distance on the map and distance on the ground.
A key (legend) explains the symbols used on a map.
The four cardinal points are north, east, south and west.
Contour lines join places of equal height above sea level.
Closely spaced contour lines show a steep slope; widely spaced lines show a gentle slope.
Grid references use eastings first and then northings.
Bearing is the direction measured clockwise from north in degrees.

example.question: On a map with a scale of 1 cm to 2 km, two towns are 6 cm apart. What is the actual distance?
example.solution: Actual distance = 6 x 2 km.
example.answer: The actual distance is 12 km.

Map Reading.summary: Maps use scale, symbols, direction and contour lines to represent real places. Reading these correctly helps you describe locations, distances and relief.

Weather and Climate.title: Introduction to Weather and Climate
Weather and Climate.introduction: Weather is the state of the atmosphere at a particular place and time, while climate is the average weather of an area over many years, usually 30 years or more.
keyConcepts: Elements of weather include temperature, rainfall, humidity, wind, pressure and cloud cover.
A thermometer measures temperature and a rain gauge measures rainfall.
A barometer measures atmospheric pressure.
Relief rainfall occurs when moist air is forced to rise over high ground, cool and condense.
Convectional rainfall is caused by strong heating of the ground, which makes warm air rise.
Latitude, altitude, distance from the sea and ocean currents affect climate.
West Africa is influenced by the tropical continental (Harmattan) and tropical maritime air masses.

example.question: Explain why temperatures usually decrease with increasing altitude.
example.solution: Air is warmed mainly by heat from the Earth's surface. Higher up the air is thinner and holds less heat, so it is cooler.
example.answer: Temperature falls with altitude because the air is thinner and further from the warm ground.

Weather and Climate.summary: Weather describes short-term conditions and climate describes long-term averages. Latitude, altitude, distance from the sea and winds all influence climate.

Rocks and Landforms.title: Introduction to Rocks and Landforms
Rocks and Landforms.introduction: The Earth's crust is made of rocks, which are shaped over time by internal and external processes. These processes create landforms such as mountains, valleys and plains.
keyConcepts: Igneous rocks form when molten rock (magma or lava) cools and solidifies.
Sedimentary rocks form from layers of sediment that are compressed and cemented over time.
Metamorphic rocks form when existing rocks are changed by heat and pressure.
Weathering is the breakdown of rocks in place.
Erosion is the wearing away and transport of rock material by wind, water or ice.
Fold mountains form when layers of rock are compressed and buckled.
A fault is a crack in the crust along which rocks have moved.

example.question: State how sandstone is formed and name its rock type.
example.solution: Sand grains are deposited in layers, compressed over a long time and cemented together.
example.answer: Sandstone is a sedimentary rock formed from compressed and cemented layers of sand.

Rocks and Landforms.summary: There are three main rock types: igneous, sedimentary and metamorphic. Weathering, erosion and movements of the crust continually shape landforms.

Basic Economic Concepts.title: Introduction to Basic Economic Concepts
Basic Economic Concepts.introduction: Economics studies how individuals, businesses and governments make choices about using limited resources to satisfy unlimited wants.
keyConcepts: Scarcity means resources are limited while human wants are unlimited.
Choice is necessary because of scarcity.
Opportunity cost is the value of the next best alternative given up when a choice is made.
The factors of production are land, labour, capital and enterprise.
Wants are things we desire; needs are things essential for survival.
A scale of preference ranks wants in order of importance.
The three basic economic questions are what to produce, how to produce and for whom to produce.

example.question: A student has GH₵50 and chooses to buy a textbook instead of a pair of sandals. What is the opportunity cost?
example.solution: The opportunity cost is the next best alternative that was given up.
example.answer: The pair of sandals.

Basic Economic Concepts.summary: Scarcity forces people to make choices, and every choice has an opportunity cost. Economics helps us understand how best to use limited resources.

Demand and Supply.title: Introduction to Demand and Supply
Demand and Supply.introduction: Demand and supply explain how prices are determined in a market. Price changes until the quantity buyers want equals the quantity sellers offer.
keyConcepts: Demand is the quantity of a good consumers are willing and able to buy at a given price.
The law of demand states that, other things being equal, a higher price reduces the quantity demanded.
Supply is the quantity of a good producers are willing to offer at a given price.
The law of supply states that, other things being equal, a higher price increases the quantity supplied.
Equilibrium price is the price at which quantity demanded equals quantity supplied.
Factors that shift demand include income, tastes, population and the prices of related goods.
Factors that shift supply include cost of production, technology and taxes or subsidies.

example.question: What happens to the equilibrium price of a good if demand increases while supply stays the same?
example.solution: A rise in demand creates a shortage at the old price, so competition between buyers pushes the price up.
example.answer: The equilibrium price rises.

Demand and Supply.summary: Prices in a market are set by the interaction of demand and supply. A change in either one moves the equilibrium price and quantity.

Money and Banking.title: Introduction to Money and Banking
Money and Banking.introduction: Money is anything generally accepted as payment for goods and services. Banks provide safe places to save money and give loans to individuals and businesses.
keyConcepts: Functions of money: medium of exchange, store of value, unit of account and standard of deferred payment.
Barter is the direct exchange of goods and services without using money.
Barter requires a double coincidence of wants, which is a major disadvantage.
A central bank manages the country's money supply, issues currency and supervises commercial banks.
Commercial banks accept deposits, give loans and provide services such as transfers.
Interest is the price paid for borrowing money or the reward for saving it.
Inflation is a general and sustained rise in the price level.

example.question: State two problems of barter trade.
example.solution: Barter needs both people to want what the other offers, and it is hard to divide or measure the value of goods.
example.answer: Double coincidence of wants and difficulty in measuring or dividing value.

Money and Banking.summary: Money makes trade easier than barter. Banks keep savings safe and provide loans, while the central bank oversees the money supply.

Pre-Colonial West Africa.title: Introduction to Pre-Colonial West Africa
Pre-Colonial West Africa.introduction: Before European colonisation, West Africa had powerful states, trading networks and rich cultures. Trade in gold, salt and other goods helped these kingdoms grow.
keyConcepts: The Ghana Empire (Wagadu) grew rich by controlling the trans-Saharan trade in gold and salt.
The Mali Empire reached its height under Mansa Musa in the 14th century.
The Songhai Empire, with its capital at Gao, became the largest of the western Sudan empires.
Timbuktu was a centre of trade, Islamic learning and scholarship.
Trans-Saharan trade linked West Africa with North Africa using camel caravans.
The Akan states, including Asante, developed in the forest zone of present-day Ghana.
Oral tradition, kept by griots and elders, preserved much of West African history.

example.question: Why was the trans-Saharan trade important to the growth of the Ghana Empire?
example.solution: Ghana's rulers controlled the gold-producing regions and taxed traders who passed through, which made the empire wealthy and powerful.
example.answer: It brought wealth through taxes on gold and salt trade, strengthening the empire.

Pre-Colonial West Africa.summary: West African empires grew through trade, strong leadership and organised government. Their cities and traditions made important contributions to African and world history.

The Atlantic Slave Trade.title: Introduction to the Atlantic Slave Trade
The Atlantic Slave Trade.introduction: The transatlantic slave trade was the forced movement of millions of Africans to the Americas between the 16th and 19th centuries. It had devastating effects on African societies.
keyConcepts: European traders built forts and castles along the coast, including Elmina and Cape Coast on the Gold Coast.
Enslaved people were transported across the Atlantic in the Middle Passage under brutal conditions.
The trade formed part of the triangular trade between Europe, Africa and the Americas.
The trade caused population loss, insecurity and wars in many African societies.
Abolitionists such as William Wilberforce and Olaudah Equiano campaigned against it.
Britain abolished the slave trade in 1807.
Its legacy includes the African diaspora and lasting social and economic effects.

example.question: State two effects of the Atlantic slave trade on West Africa.
example.solution: Millions of people were taken away, which reduced the population, and the demand for captives increased wars and insecurity.
example.answer: Loss of population and increased warfare and insecurity.

The Atlantic Slave Trade.summary: The Atlantic slave trade removed millions of people from Africa and caused lasting harm. Its abolition came through resistance by the enslaved and campaigns by abolitionists.

Colonialism and Independence.title: Introduction to Colonialism and Independence
Colonialism and Independence.introduction: From the late 19th century, European powers took control of most of Africa. In the 20th century, African people organised movements that led to independence.
keyConcepts: The Berlin Conference (1884-1885) set rules for the European partition of Africa.
Colonial rule included indirect rule and direct rule.
Colonial economies focused on exporting raw materials such as cocoa, gold and timber.
Western education and urbanisation helped produce a new educated elite.
The Gold Coast became independent as Ghana on 6 March 1957, the first sub-Saharan African country to do so.
Kwame Nkrumah and the Convention People's Party led the push for independence.
World War II and nationalism strengthened demands for self-rule.

example.question: Which leader led the Gold Coast to independence in 1957?
example.solution: Kwame Nkrumah, leader of the Convention People's Party, became the head of government and then the first leader of independent Ghana.
example.answer: Kwame Nkrumah.

Colonialism and Independence.summary: European powers divided and ruled Africa, but nationalist movements grew and won independence. Ghana's independence in 1957 inspired other African countries.

Citizenship and Rights.title: Introduction to Citizenship and Rights
Citizenship and Rights.introduction: A citizen is a person who legally belongs to a country and enjoys its rights while carrying out its duties. Rights and responsibilities help societies run fairly.
keyConcepts: A citizen can be so by birth, descent, registration or naturalisation.
Human rights are basic entitlements that every person has, such as life, liberty and equality.
Civic duties include obeying the law, paying taxes, voting and respecting others.
Fundamental human rights in Ghana's 1992 Constitution are in Chapter 5.
Rights are limited by the rights of others and by public interest.
The rule of law means everyone, including leaders, must obey the law.
Good citizens participate in community development and protect public property.

example.question: State two responsibilities of a good citizen.
example.solution: Citizens help the country to function by following its rules and contributing to the community.
example.answer: Obeying the law and paying taxes (or voting).

Citizenship and Rights.summary: Citizens enjoy rights but also have duties. A balance between rights and responsibilities supports peace, fairness and development.

Arms of Government.title: Introduction to the Arms of Government
Arms of Government.introduction: Most democratic states divide government power among three arms to prevent abuse of power. Each arm has its own functions and checks the others.
keyConcepts: The legislature makes laws; in Ghana it is Parliament.
The executive implements laws and runs the day-to-day affairs of government; it is headed by the President.
The judiciary interprets laws and settles disputes through the courts.
Separation of powers divides government functions among different bodies.
Checks and balances allow each arm to limit the powers of the others.
An independent judiciary protects citizens' rights and ensures fair trials.
A constitution is the supreme law that sets out how a country is governed.

example.question: Which arm of government interprets the law?
example.solution: Making laws is the work of the legislature and carrying them out is the work of the executive. Interpreting them in cases is done by the courts.
example.answer: The judiciary.

Arms of Government.summary: Government power is shared among the legislature, executive and judiciary. Separation of powers and checks and balances help to prevent tyranny.

Democracy and Elections.title: Introduction to Democracy and Elections
Democracy and Elections.introduction: Democracy is a system of government in which power comes from the people, who choose their leaders through free and fair elections.
keyConcepts: In a representative democracy, citizens elect people to make decisions for them.
Features of democracy include free elections, rule of law, freedom of speech and protection of rights.
Universal adult suffrage gives all eligible adult citizens the right to vote.
Political parties organise people with similar ideas and compete for power.
An electoral commission organises and supervises elections.
A secret ballot protects voters from pressure.
A free press informs citizens and holds leaders accountable.

example.question: Why is a secret ballot important in an election?
example.solution: If votes are private, voters cannot be forced or punished for how they vote, so they can choose freely.
example.answer: It protects voters from intimidation and allows them to choose freely.

Democracy and Elections.summary: Democracy depends on citizens taking part in free and fair elections. Independent institutions, a free press and respect for rights keep it healthy.

Computer Hardware and Software.title: Introduction to Computer Hardware and Software
Computer Hardware and Software.introduction: A computer is an electronic device that accepts input, processes data and produces output. It consists of hardware, the physical parts, and software, the programs that tell it what to do.
keyConcepts: Input devices include the keyboard, mouse and scanner.
Output devices include the monitor, printer and speakers.
The CPU (central processing unit) carries out instructions and is the 'brain' of the computer.
RAM is temporary memory used while the computer is on; ROM stores permanent start-up instructions.
Storage devices include hard disks, solid-state drives and flash drives.
System software, such as an operating system, manages the computer's resources.
Application software, such as word processors, helps users to carry out specific tasks.

example.question: Classify the following as input or output devices: keyboard, printer, scanner, monitor.
example.solution: Input devices send data into the computer, while output devices present results from it.
example.answer: Input: keyboard and scanner. Output: printer and monitor.

Computer Hardware and Software.summary: Hardware and software work together. Input, processing, storage and output are the basic stages of how a computer works.

Number Systems.title: Introduction to Number Systems
Number Systems.introduction: Computers store and process all data using the binary number system. Binary uses only two digits, 0 and 1, which match the on and off states of electronic circuits.
keyConcepts: The decimal system has base 10 and uses digits 0 to 9.
The binary system has base 2 and uses digits 0 and 1.
Each binary place value is a power of 2: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, and so on.
A bit is a single binary digit; a byte is 8 bits.
To convert binary to decimal, add the place values where there is a 1.
To convert decimal to binary, divide repeatedly by 2 and record the remainders in reverse order.
Hexadecimal has base 16 and uses digits 0 to 9 and letters A to F.

example.question: Convert the binary number 1011 to decimal.

Number Systems.summary: Computers use binary because it matches on/off electronic signals. Knowing how to convert between binary and decimal is a core ICT skill.

Algorithms and Programming.title: Introduction to Algorithms and Programming
Algorithms and Programming.introduction: An algorithm is a step-by-step set of instructions for solving a problem. A program is an algorithm written in a programming language that a computer can run.
keyConcepts: A flowchart uses symbols to show the steps of an algorithm.
Pseudocode describes an algorithm using simple, structured English.
Sequence means instructions are carried out one after another.
Selection (if/else) chooses between different actions depending on a condition.
Iteration (loops) repeats instructions until a condition is met.
A variable stores a value that can change while the program runs.
Debugging is finding and fixing errors in a program.

example.question: Write pseudocode to decide whether a number is positive.
example.solution: Input the number, then use selection to test whether it is greater than zero and display a message.
example.answer: INPUT n; IF n > 0 THEN PRINT 'Positive' ELSE PRINT 'Not positive'.

Algorithms and Programming.summary: Programs are built from sequence, selection and iteration. Planning with flowcharts or pseudocode makes programs easier to write and debug.

Internet and Online Safety.title: Introduction to the Internet and Online Safety
Internet and Online Safety.introduction: The internet is a global network of connected computers that lets people share information. Using it safely means protecting personal information and behaving responsibly online.
keyConcepts: A web browser, such as Chrome or Firefox, is used to view web pages.
A URL is the address of a web page.
A search engine helps you find information on the web.
Email allows messages and files to be sent electronically.
Strong passwords use a mix of letters, numbers and symbols and should not be shared.
Phishing is a trick that uses fake messages or sites to steal personal information.
Malware is harmful software such as viruses; antivirus software and updates help protect against it.

example.question: State two ways to create and use a strong password.
example.solution: A strong password is hard to guess and should be kept private.
example.answer: Use a long mix of letters, numbers and symbols, and never share it with anyone.

Internet and Online Safety.summary: The internet offers great opportunities but also risks. Strong passwords, careful clicking and safe sharing habits help keep users protected.

Soil Science.title: Introduction to Soil Science
Soil Science.introduction: Soil is the upper layer of the earth in which plants grow. It is formed by the weathering of rocks and the decay of organic matter, and its properties affect crop growth.
keyConcepts: Soil is made of mineral particles, organic matter (humus), water and air.
Soil particles are classified as sand, silt and clay.
Loamy soil is a mixture of sand, silt and clay and is generally best for crop growth.
Humus improves soil fertility and its ability to hold water.
A soil profile is a vertical section showing different layers (horizons).
Soil pH affects the availability of nutrients to plants.
Soil erosion can be reduced by terracing, contour ploughing, cover crops and mulching.

example.question: State two reasons why loamy soil is good for farming.
example.solution: Loam contains a balance of particle sizes, so it holds enough water and nutrients while allowing good drainage and aeration.
example.answer: It retains water and nutrients well and also drains and allows air into the soil.

Soil Science.summary: Soil supplies plants with water, air and nutrients. Good soil management, including protecting against erosion and adding organic matter, maintains fertility.

Crop Production.title: Introduction to Crop Production
Crop Production.introduction: Crop production is the growing of plants for food, fibre and other uses. Successful production needs good land preparation, planting, care and harvesting.
keyConcepts: Land preparation includes clearing, ploughing and harrowing.
Seeds can be planted by broadcasting, drilling or dibbling.
Crop rotation helps maintain fertility and reduces pests and diseases.
Weeds compete with crops for water, light and nutrients, and are controlled by weeding or herbicides.
Fertilisers supply nutrients: nitrogen (N), phosphorus (P) and potassium (K).
Common cash crops in Ghana include cocoa, oil palm and cashew.
Harvested crops must be dried, stored and processed properly to reduce losses.

example.question: State two advantages of crop rotation.
example.solution: Different crops use different nutrients and host different pests, so rotating them balances nutrient use and breaks pest cycles.
example.answer: It maintains soil fertility and helps control pests and diseases.

Crop Production.summary: Good crop production depends on suitable land preparation, correct planting, weed and pest control, and proper harvesting and storage.

Animal Husbandry.title: Introduction to Animal Husbandry
Animal Husbandry.introduction: Animal husbandry is the care and management of farm animals for products such as meat, milk, eggs and hides. Good housing, feeding and health care improve productivity.
keyConcepts: Ruminants, such as cattle, sheep and goats, have a complex stomach for digesting fibrous plants.
Poultry includes chickens, ducks and turkeys and is raised for meat and eggs.
Systems of rearing include free-range, semi-intensive and intensive systems.
A balanced ration supplies carbohydrates, proteins, fats, vitamins, minerals and water.
Vaccination and good hygiene help to prevent diseases.
Selective breeding improves desirable traits in animals.
Good housing protects animals from weather, predators and diseases.

example.question: Name two ruminant animals and state one advantage of intensive rearing.
example.solution: Cattle and sheep are ruminants. In intensive systems, animals are kept in confined spaces, so they are easier to feed, protect and monitor.
example.answer: Cattle and sheep; intensive rearing gives higher production and better protection from disease and predators.

Animal Husbandry.summary: Healthy, productive animals need proper feeding, housing and disease control. The system of rearing chosen affects cost, output and animal welfare.
